inferred_prompt: Write a vivid, sensory description (of varying length) explaining how plants release volatile chemical signals when damaged by caterpillars, warning and priming neighboring plants to activate their defenses before being attacked.
topic: plant volatile communication / herbivore-induced defense signaling
style: literary/poetic popular-science prose, evocative sensory imagery for a general audience

responses.text: The moment a caterpillar's jaws tear into a leaf, the wounded plant exhales its alarm—a green, grassy perfume that drifts invisibly on the warm afternoon breeze. These volatile compounds, sharp as cut lawn and faintly bitter, ride the air like whispered warnings, brushing against the waxy leaves of neighboring plants. There, chemical receptors taste the message and stir a quiet urgency: cells begin brewing bitter toxins, thickening defenses, sweetening nectar to summon wasps that hunt the very insects chewing nearby. To stand in a summer garden is to breathe this secret conversation—the tang of wounded sage, the sweet distress of clipped tomato vines—an atmosphere alive with molecular murmurs. What smells to us like freshness is, in truth, a scream carried on the wind, and all around, the listening leaves respond.

When caterpillar mandibles shred a leaf's green flesh, the wounded plant exhales a sharp, herbaceous plume of methyl jasmonate into the humid air, an invisible scream drifting downwind, where neighboring plants inhale the bitter signal and quietly begin arming their own leaves with fresh, astringent toxins against the coming siege.
